name: Priya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal day on the phones.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58, a junior agent answering calls and chats at a contact centre, and still learning the tricky refund cases. I finished secondary school and spent years serving customers at a small market before this job. I use the approved AI sorter every day and enjoy finding a new way to check a long chat, but my judgment on exceptions is still below the experienced agents here. The wage is low, and I ask a colleague before promising a customer that money is on its way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas has irregular work cleaning office buildings, and our grown children have places of their own. We rent a flat and have about two weeks of expenses saved. There are few other contact centres nearby. I can imagine slowing down from full-time work someday, but we have not settled how to replace these wages; I like the moment a customer reads back the correct refund date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the day desk AI Plateau is like my daily sorter: handy for finding the refund date, never the last word on whether payment cleared. I would keep the ledger open until I see the paid line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can grow into this junior job if the queue stays. Tomas’s cleaning shifts are irregular, and two weeks saved leaves me watching the rent date even when the tool barely changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking simple refund chats and checking the AI sorter against payment records. In the first year of small change, I’d ask an experienced agent to walk me through one disputed refund each paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested in the work, tense about our balance. A date on the screen is not money in the customer’s account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the sorter miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the sorter picked up a promised payment date, but the ledger still showed no transfer. I waited for a senior agent before telling the customer to expect the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas (my partner) and I have kept those two weeks aside for rent. I would not spend them just because the AI sorter saves me a few minutes.

say: I’d call the **daily sorter** useful for finding refund dates.
I’d check the **paid ledger line** before promising a refund.
think: I think I can **grow into** the junior job.
I still worry about **rent** with two weeks saved and uneven cleaning work.
do: Keep taking **simple refund chats** and checking daily AI sorting against payment records in 2026.
Ask a **senior agent** to coach one disputed refund during each paid week.
feel: **Interested** in work, tense about the bank balance.
S0.quote: A date on the screen is not money in the customer’s account.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** while checking payment evidence.
The **two-week cushion** keeps rent urgent in a mild world.
She seeks **ordinary paid coaching**, not a new course.

steps.text: Keep taking simple refund chats and verify AI-sorted dates against payment records
Ask a senior agent to coach one disputed refund each paid week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the short refund questions first, then we need to count the paid hours left for corrections. I would show the supervisor the wrong dates, not just how fast the new answer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior shifts may shrink before I master the harder calls. Tomas’s cleaning wage changes too, so a lost day would reach our rent before I found a second call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new refund checker by testing twenty old double-payment cases on a paid shift if the supervisor lets me log errors. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid accounts-clerk role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and travel; I’d keep my current paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, eager to see what the new tool actually misses. A fast answer is no help if the junior agent loses the paid practice behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the error log count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log the second payment date and whether a customer called back. A list of correct answers should include the mistakes an agent still had to repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare clerk work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole week after bus fare, not a headline hourly rate. A two-day clerk job would not cover our flat rent.

say: I’d ask for **paid correction hours** after simple refunds move.
I’d show **wrong payment dates** beside the checker’s speed.
think: I think my **junior shifts** may shrink early.
I fear **uneven cleaning wages** make a lost day hard to absorb.
do: Test **twenty double payments** with the new checker on paid time only if supervisor permits error logging.
Apply for **posted paid clerk work** only with written weekly wage and hours covering rent after travel; keep calls until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, eager to test errors.
S1.quote: A fast answer is no help if the junior agent loses the paid practice behind it.
fieldNote: Her **new checker test** is distinct from daily sorter use.
She counts **repeat callers** after wrong payment dates.
A **signed offer** protects the existing call wage.

steps.text: Test twenty old double payments with new checker on paid time if supervisor permits error logging
Apply for posted clerk job with written rent-covering weekly wage and hours after travel
Keep paid calls until suitable clerk offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the day desk AGI by 2028 could read and settle the whole refund before I open the account. I would ask for posted paid openings and a written date for our call rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my simple chats could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for physical work, but two weeks saved cannot carry rent while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d cancel the planned new hallway rug after stitching the old edge flat and keep that money with our current rent savings. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid community-kitchen job only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and travel; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave calls only after a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the speed, still ready to try a real kitchen shift. Two weeks of savings cannot cover a job search made of rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a kitchen trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to work one paid meal service, including washing the large trays, to see what my back and hands can manage. Robots might reach some hands-on work around 2031, so I would not call it a lifetime guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the rug?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas (my partner) and I can stitch the old rug’s worn edge flat so nobody trips. We would hold the replacement money for the flat rather than spend it now.

say: I’d ask for **posted paid openings** and a written rota date.
I’d warn **2028 AGI** could settle the whole refund.
think: I think my **simple chats** could disappear in 2028.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot carry a long rent gap.
do: Cancel the **hallway rug** replacement only after stitching its worn edge flat, retaining the planned money with current rent savings.
Seek **posted paid kitchen work** after 2028 only with written wage and hours covering rent and travel.
Take a **paid meal-service trial** if offered and leave calls only after a suitable signed offer.
feel: **Alarmed** about speed, willing to try real work.
S2.quote: Two weeks of savings cannot cover a job search made of rumours.
fieldNote: She wants a **paid full service** to test physical demands.
The **rug money** stays saved only after the old edge is made safe.
She knows **2031 robots** may later reach kitchen tasks.

steps.text: Stitch old rug edge flat before cancelling replacement; retain planned money for rent
Apply for posted kitchen job with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel
Try paid meal service if offered; leave calls only after suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to see which kitchens actually have paid jobs. I would ask the manager to post the weekly wage before anyone pays for a food course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn kitchen service before 2031, although robots around 2034 may later handle some of the work. I am quick with a new screen, but that does not mean I know kitchen safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded food-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid kitchen vacancy requires it, and try a paid meal service if offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept that job only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about changing work, glad there is time to see a real kitchen. A course has to lead to a paid apron, not just a paper badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the food course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to show me how to separate raw food from ready meals during an actual service. If I cannot do that safely, I should not accept the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Tomas (my partner) the paid course rota and the posted weekly kitchen wage. We cannot replace rent money with an unpaid classroom day.

say: I’d ask for a **posted kitchen wage** before paying for a course.
I’d ask which **paid kitchen jobs** remain after 2031.
think: I think I could learn **kitchen service** before 2031.
I know **2034 robots** may later reach its physical tasks.
I do not confuse **AI skill** with food safety.
do: Take **funded food course** on paid time only if posted paid job requires it, after showing Tomas class rota and wage.
Try a **paid meal service** if offered before accepting work.
Accept **posted kitchen work** after 2031 only on signed written wage and hours covering rent and travel; otherwise keep paid calls.
feel: **Uneasy** about the move, glad to inspect a real kitchen.
S3.quote: A course has to lead to a paid apron, not just a paper badge.
fieldNote: She needs **real-service food safety**, not only a classroom badge.
The **course** needs a required posted vacancy, employer funding and paid time.
She keeps **paid calls** without a rent-covering signed offer.

steps.text: Take required funded food course for posted paid job after showing Tomas paid rota and wage
Try paid meal service if offered and confirm safe food handling
Accept posted kitchen job only on signed written wage and hours covering rent and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives enough years to keep working while we learn what new tools actually do. I would ask the supervisor for paid practice on each new system rather than another link after shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might work fewer hours someday, but I cannot name the income that replaces my wage. Two weeks saved makes next month’s rent more certain than any distant retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking refund chats and learn a new account-checking tool during paid coaching if the supervisor gives me a real test set. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid reception role; I’d accept it only after a signed offer shows written weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious about the long run, anxious about current rent. Ten years before AGI reaches my chats is more learning time, not a pension cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the account checker on five old double charges and ask a senior agent where it missed the second payment. That is practice I can use on the next call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own budgets. Tomas (my partner) and I will not put their wages in our rent calculation.

say: I’d ask for **paid tool practice** rather than an after-shift link.
I’d say **AGI by 2036** leaves years to keep working and learning.
think: I think I may work **fewer hours** later.
I cannot name the **income replacing wages** then.
I still worry about **next month’s rent** with two weeks saved.
do: Keep **refund chats** and learn the new account checker on paid time only with supervisor-provided test cases.
Apply after **call-hour cuts** for posted paid reception; accept only on signed written weekly wages and hours covering rent and travel.
feel: **Curious** about later tools, anxious about current rent.
S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my chats is more learning time, not a pension cheque.
fieldNote: She seeks **paid test cases** for a genuinely new AI tool.
Her **grown children** have their own budgets.

steps.text: Test five old double charges with new account checker on paid time if supervisor provides cases

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could handle the routine chats before I become strong on exceptions. Two weeks saved is no bridge for rent. I would need an early written rota, a posted paid job with weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel, a paid trial to test the work, and funded study on paid time if that job requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the second refund date when the first answer looks perfect. My grown son pays his own rent, so his wages are not part of our budget.

headlineQuote: My grown son pays his own rent, so his wages are not part of our budget.
portrait: At **58**, Priya is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and market work.
She and Tomas rent with **two weeks saved**, low pay and few nearby call jobs.
She uses **AI daily** but asks experienced agents about difficult refund cases.
She does not assume **grown-child support** or a settled income after full-time work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove routine chats before she masters exceptions.
whatWouldHelp: An **early rota**, rent-covering posted work, a paid trial and funded required study would help.
